newsitem.title: USA: IPOs poor long-term investments says study.
newsitem.headline: IPOs poor long-term investments says study.

text.p: Initial public offerings make for poor long-term investments with many deals showing gains only for the few lucky investors who get in at the offering price, according to a study by Prudential Securities.
In the study of more than 1,700 new issues over the past three years, IPOs gained on average 15.6 percent from their offering price in their first trading week.
But if an investor bought at the closing price after the first day of trading, when most small investors have access, he would have lost on average of 0.2 percent.
When companies go public, Wall Street firms dish out the limited shares at the offering price to their best clients. When stock opens for sale on the exchanges, the price can often be much higher.
Fewer than half the IPOs of the past three years outperformed the Nasdaq composite index if bought at the closing price of the first day of trading, Prudential said.
Of course, few small investors are squawking about limited access to IPOs these days with razor-thin returns prevailing. But there are signs underwriters see a mild recovery on the horizon.
Last week, financier Mort Zuckerman's Boston Properties Inc. decided to brave the poor conditions, filing for the biggest IPO yet this year.
The real estate investment trust or REIT aims to raise $737.5 million, soundly beating the $386 million raised by Nationwide Financial Services Inc. in March.
The deal would also be the second biggest REIT IPO ever, just about $15 million shy of the $750 million IPO of Rockefeller Centre Properties Inc. in September 1985, according to Securities Data Co.
Qwest Communications International Inc., a Denver communications company, also filed for a $287.5 million IPO.

Bill Schreier, managing director of equity capital markets at Salomon Brothers, the lead underwriter of Qwest's IPO, said the size of deals seems to be growing because investors are demanding larger deals that offer higher liquidity.
"Investors are much more concerned now about getting into an illiquid position, because in case of a market correction, if you're a fund manager, you need to be about to raise cash quidkly," he said.

"(The market) is starting to become more optimistic. The bond market rallied quite a bit as people think perhaps the Fed may not act in May and stocks have followed suit ... There's a growing sense the worst may be behind us," he said.
Last week, the Dow Jones Industrials rose nearly 315 points to end at 6,703.55 Friday.
For now, IPOs remains stifled. Last week, eight firms went public raising $392 million, according to Securities Data.
Few posted gains and next week should be more of the same, said John Fitzgibbon, editor of the IPO Aftermarket.
"Pickings are slim with most of the deals small-cap issues by small underwriters," he said.
